blocks.content: Beyond the basics covered in the ARG instruction topic, build arguments have real rules around scoping and a few practical gotchas worth knowing, especially around secrets.
1. Overriding a Default at Build Time
blocks.text: 1. Overriding a Default at Build Time

blocks.content: An ARG declared with a default value in the Dockerfile can be overridden per build with --build-arg, without ever touching the Dockerfile itself, exactly the mechanism a CI pipeline uses to inject a version number or a git commit hash into a build.

blocks.alt: A default value, freely overridden per build

blocks.content: In a multi-stage build, an ARG declared before the first FROM, or inside one stage, is not automatically visible in a later stage, each stage that actually needs the value has to redeclare ARG itself, a genuinely common source of confusion when a value "disappears" partway through a build.

blocks.alt: Each stage needing the value must redeclare ARG itself

blocks.content:
ARG VERSION=1.0

FROM golang AS builder
ARG VERSION
RUN echo "Building $VERSION"

FROM alpine
ARG VERSION
LABEL version=$VERSION

code.content:
ARG VERSION=1.0

FROM golang AS builder
ARG VERSION
RUN echo "Building $VERSION"

FROM alpine
ARG VERSION
LABEL version=$VERSION

codes.dockerfile:
ARG VERSION=1.0

FROM golang AS builder
ARG VERSION
RUN echo "Building $VERSION"

FROM alpine
ARG VERSION
LABEL version=$VERSION

blocks.content: BuildKit automatically provides certain ARGs without you declaring them, most notably TARGETPLATFORM and TARGETARCH, useful when building multi-architecture images (x86 and ARM from the same Dockerfile) that need to branch behavior per target platform.
4. Never Pass Secrets as Build Arguments
blocks.text: 4. Never Pass Secrets as Build Arguments

blocks.content: This is a real, common mistake: a value passed via --build-arg gets recorded in the image's build history, anyone with access to the image can potentially retrieve it later, even if it was never explicitly ENV'd. Secrets should use BuildKit's dedicated --secret flag instead, which mounts the value only for the duration of a specific instruction and never persists it in a layer.

blocks.alt: Build args leak into history, BuildKit secrets never persist

blocks.content:
# Bad: this API key ends up in the image's build history
docker build --build-arg API_KEY=supersecret .

# Better: BuildKit secret, never written to any layer
docker build --secret id=apikey,src=./apikey.txt .

code.content:
# Bad: this API key ends up in the image's build history
docker build --build-arg API_KEY=supersecret .

# Better: BuildKit secret, never written to any layer
docker build --secret id=apikey,src=./apikey.txt .

codes.bash:
# Bad: this API key ends up in the image's build history
docker build --build-arg API_KEY=supersecret .

# Better: BuildKit secret, never written to any layer
docker build --secret id=apikey,src=./apikey.txt .

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: ARG scope is per-stage in a multi-stage build, a value has to be redeclared in every stage that actually needs it.
Never pass secrets via --build-arg, they persist in the image's build history, use BuildKit's --secret flag instead.
